subject: Biology
title: Natural Selection and Behavior
description: A micro-lesson that makes Natural Selection and Behavior usable.

hook.text: A peacock's extravagant tail makes it slower and more visible to predators. So why does it exist?

buildup.text: Natural selection favors behaviors and traits that increase reproductive success.

discovery.text: The peacock's tail signals genetic fitness. Peahens choose males with the most impressive displays.

twist.text: Even seemingly harmful behaviors persist if they help an animal pass on its genes.

climax.text: Every animal behavior—from courtship dances to alarm calls—has been shaped by survival pressure.

punchline.text: If it helps you reproduce, evolution keeps it.

quiz.question: Why do peacocks have extravagant tails?
options: They signal genetic fitness to peahens

details.summary: Natural selection shapes behavior just as it shapes physical traits. Behaviors that increase survival and reproduction are passed to future generations. Foraging strategies, predator avoidance, and social behaviors all evolve under selection pressures.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding that behavior evolves through natural selection is the foundation of behavioral ecology. It explains why animals behave optimally in their environments and why behavior changes when environments shift.
takeaways: Behaviors with genetic components can be selected for or against
Optimal foraging theory predicts how animals should choose food sources
Behavioral traits evolve in response to specific ecological pressures

faq.question: How can natural selection act on behavior?
faq.answer: Behaviors influenced by genes can be inherited. If a foraging strategy leads to better nutrition and more offspring, genes underlying that strategy increase in frequency. Over generations, populations evolve more efficient behavioral patterns.

faq.question: Does all animal behavior have a genetic basis?
faq.answer: Most behaviors involve both genetic predisposition and environmental influence. Pure learning without any genetic basis is rare, as is pure instinct without any environmental input. The interaction between genes and environment produces behavioral variation.
